utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honour. Before I start, I'd just would seek your leave to make one submission, very brief submission. The submission is pursuant to Rule 73, and it's an application to add two exhibits to the Prosecution's exhibit list. The first exhibit is a medical record that pertains to this witness, and it's a record of her injury that we submit was caused by a mortar shell. And in terms of disclosure, I have disclosed this medical record to the Defence as soon as I received it. And the reason why it was not on the original exhibit list is because the witness brought it to us the day she arrived for testimony. I submit that the exhibit is probative and relative and the Defence have had due notice of the exhibit and, therefore, I would ask that it be added to the exhibit list. The second exhibit is a set of photographs provided by the next witness to attend here. Again, the witness brought these photographs with him during the proofing session, and they have been disclosed to dually to the Defence. The photographs pertain to the observation point one and various other locations in Sarajevo; and for this reason, I submit is that these photographs are also probative. And, therefore, we ask that this -- these photographs be added to the exhibit list. I understand the Defence have been notified, and I understand they do not have an objection to the variation of the exhibit list. Those would be my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me hear from Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm going to deal with this witness. Regarding the medical report, if it is exhibit number ERN 0606-9970, we have no objection regarding this document. This is the exhibit that was disclosed to us. Now regarding the photographs, I believe it is my colleague that is going to deal with them because he is the one that is going to use these photographs. Your Honour, regarding the photographs, Defence has no objection regarding these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, just on the identification of the -- the medical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic said she had no objection if the exhibit was number ERN 0606-9970. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we -- we'll accede to your submission that they be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, before I start, I just want to tell that you have asked for protection, and the Court has granted you protective measures in the -- in the name of voice and face and pseudonym. And, therefore, during my examination, I will refer to you as Witness 107, and you should be careful not to state anything that could identify you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Firstly, I'm going to show you a piece of paper, and on this piece of paper should be your personal details. I'd like you to look at this piece of paper and confirm to the Court whether these personal details are correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Those are my details. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P349, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you presently live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I live at Grbavica in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the conflicts and prior to the conflict, did you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: We lived before the conflict at Grbavica, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the conflict, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I stayed at home, I was a housewife, I was in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Apart from a housewife -- being a housewife, were you involved in any other activities during the time in Sarajevo during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: While I was at Grbavica, I wasn't doing anything much. Later when I crossed over to the other side, I was in the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When did you leave from Grbavica to the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: 26th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Serb forces, the police and soldiers, barged into our apartment two or three times a day and night, and they mistreated us. My husband was not there, so they barged in whenever they wanted. My husband had to go to Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What did your husband do at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: My husband was wanted by the Serb army. They wanted to look at his document. He couldn't report. On the 25th, he did report, and they said if he doesn't come, they will take away me and my daughters. My older daughter was 25; the other one was 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was your husband in the military, or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: He was a civilian working with the army before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the war, was he in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: He was with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just going back to your answer where you said, "the Serb forces, the police and soldiers, barged into our apartment two or three times a day," what did they say to you when they came into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: They told us what were we doing there? Where is my husband? I said he had gone to fetch some food. They said, "Your people are on the other side. You've got no business being here. You should go to Alija's state."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How long did this last for? In other words, how many times did the -- how many times did the -- did the police and soldiers come to your apartment, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Regularly, and even the neighbours invited me to say that the police had come and soldiers in my absence. The legal army -- the legal ones searched two or three times a day, searching for weapons, and the other ones were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said, "Serb forces, the police and soldiers." How did you know that these people were Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: My building faced Vraca. On the 2nd of May, they came, they had white bands, they came in vehicles with tarpaulins, they barged in with masks on their faces, they devastated and destroyed -- did all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the question that was asked you was: How were you able to identify those people as Serb forces? How did you know that they were Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they barged in while Grbavica was occupied. They were all troops of the Republika Srpska army. They forced us -- they trying to make us to go to the other side. They were saying it was the Serb state there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you in fact move to the other side then, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: We left on the 26th May when they threatened that they would take us to Kula and Lukavica. They said that me and my older daughter could not stay in the apartment, no way, and they made us go. So I left with my two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where did you move to? And if you could just tell me the district and possibly the building, but don't provide the number of the house or the flat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: We crossed over the market to the small bridge because the big bridge, the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge, was under fire by snipers. We left while the troops were being inspected. Every ten metres you would see troops wearing helmets and with their vehicles nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Maybe my question wasn't precise enough. Where did you go to live after that? In which district in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: We left for Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And don't tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you say TMP? What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: It's TMP. It's the B/C/S acronym for the Square of International Friendship, Trg Medjunarodnog Prijateljstva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, when you moved to Alipasino Polje, you had earlier said that you started to work for the civil defence. Can you tell the Court whether the civil defence was a military or a civilian institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: It was a civilian institution. They were working for the civilians supplying them with medicines, firewood, food, humanitarian aid arrived there. I was cleaning there. It was all for civilians, for the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you work for the civil defence in the period August 1994 through to November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I worked with the civilian defence from the 1st of July, 1992, until 1996, at least I was on record in that period as working there. I ran away from Grbavica and signed up within a month with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In relation to where you lived in Alipasino Polje, where was the civil defence office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: It was close to where I lived. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. Could we have that identification of the flat number redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness 107, I want to take you to the 30th of August, 1992. Do you remember an incident on that date, the 30th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness. Would the usher please make sure that the microphone is turned on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Witness 107, because your voice is distorted, it is important that you speak into the microphone whenever answering a question. So my question, again, is do you remember an incident on the 30th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: On the 30th of August, there was an incident at the market, at Alipasino Polje while we were queuing for bread. There were about 100 of us. We were just waiting in line. It was 11.00, 11.30. A shell mowed us down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say there were about 100 of us, what kinds of people there were? Were they children, women, military personnel, civilian personnel? Can you describe the crowd to the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: There were children, elderly men, not so many young people. There were no soldiers, only civilians who were trying to buy some bread to survive, just like I did. All sorts of people, young and old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you recall the weather on that day, at the time that you were waiting in the square there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: There was no rain. It was a bit overcast but there was no rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What time did you get to the square to start queuing for the bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I went twice. I went once at 8.00. They told me to come back at 9.00 because the bread would come then. So I walked back to my apartment which wasn't far away and then I went again at 10.00, 10.15. They told me it would be coming soon, so I queued up, and I was waiting in line when the shell fell. We were all mowed down. There was screaming, moaning. It was a harrowing sight, something indescribable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that you went home and then came back again. How far was this square from your home, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Well, a kilometre, perhaps; 800 metres, perhaps. I don't know exactly, but not far. It was -- the market was just across the street from the television building. It was the Solidarity Square.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the time that you were there, in other words from the first time to the second time and until the shell landed, did you notice any military personnel, any military installations in the vicinity of the square at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: There were no troops. There were no military installations or buildings. There were only civilians. People struggling to survive, trying to buy whatever they could lay their hands on at market, because we had been encircled in Sarajevo from all sides, and we were under fire from all sides. Everybody shot at us constantly, like beasts. They were trying to kill as many of us as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that you were waiting in line and the shell fell. If you can -- if you're able to, can you describe what happened to you when the shell landed; but very briefly, if possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: When the shell landed, I suddenly felt something pressing on my chest, like I was breathing into a barrel; and then I thought another and another would come because they always fell in threes, but this time luckily it was only one shell. Still it had mowed us down. I couldn't breathe. I felt like a barrel trying to breathe, trying to walk. I couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you sustain injuries as a result of this shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I sustained injuries to my lungs, my diaphragm, my liver. Everything from my chest to my back was injured, destroyed. I have 60 per cent invalidity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you go to -- well, were you admitted into hospital; and if you were, for how long did you remain in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Some people picked us up, took us to the hospital where I spent a month; 30 days, I think. Yes, a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 03030, and could I ask that it not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, in a moment, if you look at your screen, there should be a document that has appeared. Do you see a document there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: This is my discharge document from the hospital, 30th of August 1992. I can never forget that. My lungs and my chest are full of shrapnel. Only I know how I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P350, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, lastly, on this incident, Witness 107, did you know or did you find out as to whether other people were injured or deceased from this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: There was a boy, Dejan in intensive care unit. When his mother came to visit him, he said that 20 people were killed and 35 other people were simply thrown into the air by the shell. And that little boy, Dejan, he also had shrapnel in his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I want to take you to the 16th of June, 1995. Do you remember an incident on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: The 16th of June can never be forgotten. I was on duty at the local commune. We took turns in duty service, about 30 of us. I was on duty on that day with two of my colleagues. At 1530, we heard the sound of an aeroplane, or the sound like an aeroplane flying through the room. We were all thrown into the air and thrown to different sides, different corners of the room. We were lying on the floor when somebody called Dzemo came to see what had happened to us. We were then taken to a shelter. Later they told me it was an air bomb. I said, "What do you mean air bomb? It had to be a whole aeroplane hitting us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection regarding the transcript. I heard the witness saying earlier the command -- the major came, and I'm not seeing this; and then a person called Dzemo came with the major, and this is not on the transcript. Maybe we could check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness. Witness, would you just repeat what you said in relation to the-- a Major coming.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Not a major; it was a commander. We had this senior person. He was a civilian. He was with the civil defence. He was our commander, and he ordered people us what to do and made the schedules. And we had to obey him, his orders. He worked for the civilian defence. He was our commander. Commanding officer, "komandir," that's what we called him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I have a question to check if something is accurate. In the English, I am reading what follows: "[In English] Local commune." [Interpretation] What exactly is this "local commune?" What kind of institution is it? Is it an office? What kind of place is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a building where the humanitarian aid was unloaded and commissioners came there for food. Everything was there. The Red Cross and the -- such organisations. We were there to help the civilians out. We had a roll call every morning at 8.00 there. We had to listen to the orders and comply with the orders for the civilians; what was to be done with the wounded, what was to be done with the humanitarian aid that was being distributed, and we all did such humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this sort of bomb fell on that very building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This bomb fell by the building, some ten metres from the place where we were on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to be clear. The place where you worked, did -- well, were there ever soldiers at that place? People who had weapons, people who had uniforms, or was it simply a place with civilians. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not the "or," because that is leading. Just ask her what kind of place it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No. There were no soldiers there. There were only civilians there from around the area where the people lived. We would gather there in the shelters. The people who had been band -- banished, they came, and there was no troops or soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were the recipients of your aid and your work, were they civilians or were they soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: They were all civilians, civilians who were given humanitarian relief. We had to know how many members there were. This Alipasino Polje local community had some 40.000 nationals, and that is where we worked in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the place where you worked and where you lived, in the vicinity were there any military installations or facilities nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No, none. No military facilities at all; only civilians. People who lived in these buildings and people from the surrounding area, they would come to that local commune, and they would report and would be distributed humanitarian aid. Everything was makeshift. Everything would be made. We had nothing. We didn't have any fuel, any wood for fires. We didn't have any stoves. So we sought to help the elderly. Whatever was required, we would take to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Commissioners would come. A commissioner would come to the local commune, and he would say such-and-such does not have water, does not have a cooking range, or something similar. So our people would go out and seek to help such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you started to tell us about how you heard the sound of an aeroplane. Did you hear this aeroplane or -- well, did you hear it land and explode? Let me ask you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: We were in the local community and we heard the aeroplane sound, and I had a feeling that the plane had actually impacted the building because we were all thrown around. That was the feeling I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you or any of your colleagues sustain any injuries as a result?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I actually don't know what happened to me. I had some scratches on some parts of my body, on the forehead, and I was all swollen. Actually, I was wounded in the right side of my body. I only remember that there were moans and screams all over the place, and everybody was on one another in the shelter; the children, the small babies, all the people. I was there for five days -- three or five days. I don't remember; day and night. We slept on some blankets. All I recall is the moaning and the screaming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say that you went to the shelter. When did you go to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: My colleagues actually took me there when Rasim, the komandir, the commanding officer came, and Dzemo also came. And they took me down to the shelter and there we lay on some crates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you go to the shelter after the explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: After the explosion when they picked us up. And when this Rasim,, who we called commander, came, they asked us, "People are you alive?" And they pulled us from under the debris, and they pulled us out and then they took us to the shelter. They took me to the shelter. I don't know what happened to the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say they -- they "pulled us from under the debris." Did the civil defence --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: They took us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The place where you worked, did it sustain damage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: This was a building which had wood panels on the walls. It was all destroyed. It all fell out of the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How far was the shelter from the place you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: The shelter was not far. It was five metres or ten metres around the corner. You just had to go around the corner and the shelter was right there. There was some crates and some packing material in the shelter. So we spent about five days or three or five days, I'm not quite sure, on those crates. I don't know when it was day and when it was night, because it was dark all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you a photograph, and I'm going to ask you some questions about the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If 65 ter 03031 could be shown on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a photograph there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, I see it all. I can see where I was, where I worked, where I went to the shelter. I can see it all before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would actually like to do this in open session. But just to be in the safe side, I'm going to ask her to make some markings, so perhaps this should be done in private session. Or I can see how I proceed and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's try that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you identify the place where the civilian defence was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: This is where the civilian defence was here. There is a passage and a door, right here. Here, this is the entrance. This was the entrance to our local community centre, local commune centre, where we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Just put a cross there, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you see the place where the shelter is on that photograph; and if you can, just put the letter S where the shelter was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: The shelter was here on the other side. This is where we entered the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I was going to ask you if you could mark the place where the -- the projectile landed, but perhaps -- perhaps I'll tender this first, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It landed on the other side, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit P351, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I ask that 03033 be brought up on the screen, please. I hope this is the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, is this a photograph that -- a better photograph for you to identify where the projectile landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: On the other side, there is a meadow. It is not here. It is not this. There is a meadow there, and it is on the other side that the projectile landed. This is the entrance to the buildings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, on this photograph, can you see a part of the meadow on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No, you can't see it. You cannot see here. Behind the green building, there is a large spacious meadow; and, in fact, there are two entrances to the local commune centre, on this side and on the other side where I already marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see on this photograph, in the middle of the photograph, do you see a tree there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is a park, and there is a big meadow behind it and there is the cemetery behind it; and then there is a still a part of the local commune after it. It was a huge local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you say that "there is a big meadow behind it," is that the meadow that you speak about, where the projectile landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: That is right. You cannot see it on this picture. It is on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P352, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, lastly, I would like to ask that 65 ter 00312 to be brought up on the screen, and, again, for it not to be broadcast. And it's the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a document there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we zoom it up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it. It is a list of my comrades with whom I was on duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that that part needs to be redacted. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I would redact it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I would tender this under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as Exhibit P353, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's just the first page for the benefit of the court deputy -- the second page. Sorry, excuse me. And that is the examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. My name is Branislava Isailovic, and I am representing the general who is accused before this Trial Chamber, General Milosevic. I would like to ask you a certain number questions regarding, first of all, what you have stated in your examination-in-chief, and I would like to start with two statements that you gave to the OTP. Do you recall, first of all, giving statements to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement to the OTP on the 12th of March, 1997 [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I gave these statements in Nedzarici, but I do not know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I would like to ask that the statement be put on the screen with all the necessary precautions of course, and I'm talking about the document DD00-1391.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that document be placed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the screen you can see the cover page of this statement. Can you tell us if you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you see your signature at the bottom of the page, on the English version, of course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's move to the second page of this document, please, and I would like to ask you a question regarding this document. In the third paragraph of this statement, you talk about the Territorial Defence for which you worked. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that. Territorial Defence, that is civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, the Territorial Defence for you is the same thing as civil protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Witness, who told you that the Territorial Defence was the name of the place where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: When I fled from Grbavica to Alipasino Polje, I went to the community and I signed up. I reported and it was the TO then. And they assigned us to different tasks, to clean, to help out the people. That was the TO which was attached to the municipal centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, who was your employer? Was it the Territorial Defence, the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No. It may have been the TO, but he was our commanding officer for civilian affairs. That's how we called him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, to be very clear, you were paid for the work that you did; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No, no. We were not paid at all. We didn't get any salaries. We were given some food. There was no salary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you had medical insurance at that time from your employer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: What medical insurance? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have at the time a -- an ID card, a card that allowed you to have medical insurance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No. We didn't have anything of the kind. It was war. There was nothing. We worked for the people. People were getting killed. We struggled to survive and to see to it that people got some necessities to clean up, to help people, including by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement in the same paragraph, you stated that you -- that you had to bring messages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Messages would come to the local commune. We had people working for the Red Cross so that messages would come there and would be distributed to the people who were the addressees. The messages started coming in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. But would you please read to us that paragraph. Could you please read paragraph number 3 where you said: "I started working."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you see the paragraph beginning: "I started working with the Territorial Defence." That's the paragraph which you are being asked to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "I started working with the Territorial Defence at the community centre." This was not the community centre. This was a civilian defence facility. I would do anything that I was asked to do; cooking, cleaning, or taking messages. I did cleaning there, and people brought messages there. There was not an a community centre in the sense of a community house. It was the local commune centre. There would be messages brought in when there was a lot of shooting, when there was heavy fighting, when there were alarms sounded for the people in order for the people not to move about and such.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, if I understood you correctly, you were sort of a person who -- or, actually, the office where you worked was sort of a place where messages were brought to people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Time, sometimes I would go to see the other commander down there in the municipality. I would go back immediately after having delivered a letter, but this happened just once or twice. But most of the time I would do cleaning and scrubbing work, after four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, above the paragraph that you just read, you state how you fled Grbavica and you describe how you went over the bridge, Bratstva Jedinstva. It's in the second paragraph at the very end of that paragraph. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No, I don't see it. I know that it is the Square of Brotherhood and Unity, Bratstva Jedinstva. I know that I crossed the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That -- if you look at the your statement at the end of the second paragraph, there is a sentence that starts with: "I saw an old man get close to the control checkpoint."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Oh, yes. When we fled away, when we set off from Grbavica after we had gone by the market, we ran across a Serb-manned checkpoint, and my daughter asked me where should we go, and I -- and I said we have to follow this elderly man. So this guy actually didn't ask me much. We passed by the Square of Brotherhood and Unity to the little bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, today, you told us a story that is slightly different from what you said in your statement. What you said in your statement is that a true account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Everything is true. It is true that it all happened. One can never forget it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What you're telling us in that paragraph of your statement, that is exactly how the events took place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Precisely the way I said it. It all happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, may I conclude, therefore, that you were not asked any questions. You went own the other side of the bridge across the bridge, and nobody controlled you. Nobody check the you. You didn't have it go through a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes. We did go through the checkpoint, through one checkpoint. There was one checkpoint that everybody had to pass through. Every 20 metres, there is were army troops. We followed that old man who said to the people at the checkpoint that he was going to the bakery, and we followed after him and passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this, of course, was in the presence of the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's move to your second statement from the 17th of May, 2005. It's DD00-1397.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this statement is not broadcasted. Good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to you take a look at this document and tell us if you see your signature at the bottom of the cover page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall that you saw somebody from the OTP a second time on that date, that you gave the statement on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: When was this? I can't see properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 17th of May, 2005.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know the dates of my statements. All I know is that I went to give them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to page number 3, and in both versions the paragraph that I'm looking for is the paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So please take paragraph 14 and tell us, first of all, when you answered to some questions that the Prosecutor put to you, you mentioned that you left Grbavica and you talked about it. Do you recall? Just an objection to correct the transcript. I mentioned you talked about some days that preceded your departure. I would just like the transcript to reflect my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Isailovic, also on page 24, you talked about paragraph 14 in both versions. I think that it's in the second version. It's in the second statement that you are looking for that paragraph, paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it's page number 3 of both versions, because sometimes the B/C/S version and the English version is not the same. But now we're on the same page. It's page number 3 of both the B/C/S and English version, and I would like you to take a look at paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you talked about soldiers who came to harass you in a certain way. They would come to your apartment in Grbavica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see the answer from the witness or maybe she didn't answer. The question has been asked and there is no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked whether you talked about soldiers who would harass you in a certain way, and that they would come to your apartment in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Soldiers came to our apartment, both by day and by night, and harassed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Still talking about the same paragraph, paragraph 14. At the very beginning of this paragraph, you talk about this, and I hope of course this document is not broadcasted. You did not, however, mention your street. I would like you to -- or actually do not tell us the name of the street. Your address is there but do not tell -- to not tell us where you lived. I would just like to you take a look at this paragraph and tell us, confirm to us that this was your address?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, it is. All that in that paragraph is correct. That's my statement, and that's my address, the former and the current address.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is why I am asking you to not tell us your street name, do not give us your address. Please tell us, is it right to say this was a high-rise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Those were five-storey military pavilions, military buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we move into private session for just a few seconds. I would just like to make sure that the address it not given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us if you remember if there were some military activities at that time, before you left Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, close to the stadium there was street fighting involving rifles, infantry weapons. The shooting went on day and night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Where you lived at the time, that area, was it very close to the lines where that fighting went on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Well, it was about a kilometre away, maybe kilometre and a half. There were tanks across from me. Close to the Drvo Rijeka building, there was one tank there and another tank close to the shopping centre. They would occasionally fire. All the glass windows were shattered. We didn't dare sleep in our apartment. We slept in the neighbour's apartment because the neighbour had left for Lukavica. He left us the keys and said, "If you need, you can spend the night there," and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, according to you, it was very dangerous for civilians to stay in that neighbourhood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Exactly. Because they persecuted us and they barged into our apartments. When the tanks fired, all the glass was shattered, although they were firing to the other side, not at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, still in the same paragraph, you said that you telephoned your husband. You called your husband on the phone. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, we called him when the military police had been to see us. They wanted to see his ID. They would come three or four times a day looking for my husband. They said they just wanted to look at his papers, so he called back on the 26th of May. My husband Zoran called me, and I passed the receiver to that man so that they can reach agreement. And they agreed that the next day at 10.00 they would meet at the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge, that my younger daughter would go and Zoran would go so they don't shoot. They said they just wanted to look at his personal ID. But that night I decide to the escape and that's what I did. The next morning at 7.00, I fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Witness, your husband called you in Grbavica. He called your apartment in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: He called us at our apartment in Grbavica. He was at Kobilja Glava at my brother's. He called me on the 25th of May. Zoran was in my apartment when he called, and they agreed that he should come down -- that he would come down and look at my husband's papers; that my daughter would come along, too; that they would meet on the bridge; and that nothing else would happen. They would just look at his papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that Zoran, was he a soldier, a Serb soldier from the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Well, possibly. He was in camouflage uniform. They had caps on their heads. They must have been Serbs. I called up my neighbour, and he said, "We have nothing to do with it." He said, "MUP had nothing to do with it. It's the military police."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the very end of the paragraph, you mentioned that the Serb soldiers took your jewellery and property, your goods. Can you explain to us what happened exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be precise, the paragraph at least in the English version, does not say that the Serb soldiers took her jewellery. It says that the Serb soldiers were breaking into apartments taking jewellery and property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Precisely so, in the English at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, can you please tell us what happened to you? What happened in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Soldiers would come to our place. They barged in to our apartment looking for weapons. They carried away whatever they wanted; drinks, any kind of spirits, all the bottles that were not opened. They even looked into pots and pans.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you knew this because this was the case for your apartment? They took something from the kitchen in your apartment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: They took pots and pans from our kitchen. One thing that my husband got as a price, they said it was good so they took it away. We had an unopened bottle of spirits; they took that away. Somebody said it was the -- not the legal army, and we shouldn't open the door but we didn't dear not to open. We were afraid not to. They were armed. If they were knocking on your door carrying rifles, of course, I had to open. Other people didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the Prosecutor used 40 minutes, and you have so far used 30 minutes. So you may go to the -- to the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, so after you left, you went to Alipasino Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And today you mentioned that you changed, if I understood you correctly, apartments; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, those apartments where you moved, because you lived there for a while, were those empty apartments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Those were vacant apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know who used to live there at the time? For example, did neighbours tell you who used to live there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, I know. We were told. I know who lived there before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And who used to live there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Can I say who lived there before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we should move into private session. Maybe it would be more prudent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please indicate to us the area where the shell landed on the 16th of July, 1995, and please you can make a circle at that place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Behind this green building, it fell at the corner of this building, onto the clearing. I can't show is it here. It fell on the other side. There was another entrance here to the local commune centre, and the second entrance. There were two entrances to the local commune. It fell on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you maybe just indicate to us the side where, with respect to the high-rise building, the area or the side where the shell landed somehow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Well, if you go down this building, there is a clearing behind this building. I cannot show it to you, because it's behind the building. If you showed me the other side, I would be able to mark it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, for the transcript, may I help you by saying the following, that with respect to this picture, the area in question is-- or the place where the shell landed would be behind the building on top of the picture where we see the basketball field. Is that where the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: The shell fell behind this building. There is a clearing there, and the cemetery is on the same side. You cannot see it from this building here. The clearing is over there. It fell on the edge of the asphalt path next to another entrance of our local commune. I can't see it from here, from this building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: May I, therefore, conclude that it's behind the tallest high-rise and in the direction of the basketball field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes. This building here, there's clearing over there. Behind this green building there, it fell -- I don't know, do you have a different view of this area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Her answer contains information about this building and that building. Perhaps it could be brought out exactly which building she is talking about. It's my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Witness, would you tell us had a building you're referring to when you say that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This entrance into the local commune; this was the building of the local commune. There is one entrance from the clearing and once entrance from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you mark it for us, mark the building that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where the entrance was, and there was another entrance on the other side of the building where the shell landed, from the clearing. That's where the shell landed. There are two entrances to the local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have already placed an X at the -- at the entrance. Do you remember that? You placed an X to the entrance to the building. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an entrance to the local commune here, but there is another entrance where the air bomb landed. But we can't see that other entrance from this being. It's in the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I think we have an idea now of the building that she's referring to. It would seem to me that it's the same building in relation to which she has marked the X, but there is no view of it in this photograph. There is no view of the place where the shell fell in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no view, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I precisely asked a question to the witness, and the witness answered that it's, in fact, behind the tallest building, between the tall building and the basketball field, and the witness already replied by saying yes. Now, regarding the day, the 16th of June, regarding that date, did you notice --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No, no. Not up there. It's not there. It's behind this building where the basketball court is, where basketball is played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But can you see the basketball court. Is the basketball court visible in this photograph, Witness? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I have asked you whether you can see the basketball court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was up there above the buildings; the basketball court. That's not where the shell landed. It landed on the other side of this high-rise building, and there is no way that I can show it to you because I cannot see it on this photograph. It is on the other side of the clearing, on the other side of the meadow. I can't show it from had position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it's still the same question. If we look at this picture, we have two groups of buildings. One that is comprised of two buildings. In the forefront and in the background, there are two other buildings. Is that right? So we have two possibilities. With the second set of buildings that is in the background, you have the first part of the building that is taller; and behind that building, the tallest building, there is a basketball field. You said that is not where -- you said that's where the shell fell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not land up there. It is behind this building, the lawn, the meadow behind this first building, and it fell near the entrance to the local commune, the second entrance to the local commune which I cannot show you on this photograph. That is where the air bomb landed. The entrance to the local commune, if you have another photograph, I could show you. So it's in the meadow behind this building that I'm unable -- and I'm unable to show you the exact spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, could I cross-examine for five more minutes before the break? It's very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, so we're talking about the 16th of June, you recall that day. Do you recall when you went to work on that day? Do you know if there was any military activities, intense military activities going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: It wasn't near us. It was in the vicinity of Ilidza and thereabouts. We could hear the infantry fire, but it wasn't near here. What we had there were just shells. There was snipers in some places in Nedzarici and in the approaches.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told to go to the shelter? Did you get a warning saying that you had to go to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: After the air bomb landed, I was taken to the shelter and there was this screaming and moaning and shouting by people, and I didn't know anything from that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question was different. On that day, in the morning, on June 16, had you been told that you should go to the shelter for the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I didn't in fact know about that shelter being there at all. Nobody told us about it until that particular incident. There was a roll call every morning at 8.00, and we would be assigned to our representative duties; to clean, to help people, to see who needed what, water, cooking ranging, queue in lines, and take whatever was needed to the people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please not overlap with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The layout?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're going asked not to overlap with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So regarding the layout of that area, there is a lot of high-rises in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And Mojmilo hill is very close; it's what separates the part that could be called --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So it separates. So we have Alipasino Polje, Mojmilo hill, and then you have got Lukavica right behind, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And towards Nedzarici there are also high-rises that are very similar to the ones that we see on the photograph, a great number of high-rises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: If this here is Alipasino Polje, this is where I was. I didn't go to Nedzarici. We did not dare go to Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. But the street where there's the trolley-bus, the street is close to Nedzarici. But are there a lot of high-rises in Alipasino Polje, in that area of Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yeah, there are. There are high-rise buildings. There are also less-tall buildings. They are not very many high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The high-rises over there don't look like the ones here on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I didn't really look. I know that my daughter lived here on the second floor and my brother on the fourth. I was on the tenth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: One last question. These flats had been freed because Serbs had left them. You're saying that all members in your family were living in different flats, and they all had been left by Serbs that had left the area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No. My brother was living in his own apartment, and my daughter lived with the family that she had married into. Some Serbs had left their apartments, some hadn't. I mean there were all sorts of things going on at the time. The commissioners were all assigned each to one entrance. The commissioners were people in charge. They had lists of people in each entrance. There were Croats and Muslims and Serbs living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I haven't stopped you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know of any Serbs who left apartments in which they were living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know just about this person where I lived. I know that he left. I heard that he had worked on television and that he had left for Republika Srpska. He worked for the Srna agency. There he gave statements there. He recorded things and that was -- that was the statement he gave to Srna, but he worked for BH Television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know why he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why he left. I know why I did what I did. I don't know why other people did what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, do you have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am finished with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to have two statements offered into evidence, DD00-1391 and DD00-1397. These are the two statements made by the witness, and I would like to have them offered into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We add met them under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those will be admitted-- well, document number DD00-1391, the statement from 12 March, 1995 will be admitted under seal as D115. Document DD00-1397, statement from 17th May 2005 will be admitted as D116, both under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a couple of questions. We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I ask the court deputy to have on the screen P351, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 107, just a couple of more questions and then I will conclude. I'm taking you back to this photograph. Do you see the photograph on your screen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I take on board that you have -- your evidence is that you can't see the location where the shell -- the air bomb landed. But what I'd like you to do is, with the use of an arrow, can you draw an arrow point -- just listen to me carefully. Are you able to draw an arrow pointing to the place, even if it is behind the building or obstructed, to the place where you think the air bomb land? Are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Yes. At the angle of this building, actually here, behind the top of this tall high-rise building, where on the other side where the meadow is was the entrance who the local community centre. It was at the very corner of this building. Do you have a photograph showing the view of the other side? Because I am unable to do that on this one. So this asphalt is also on the other side of the building. I can't show you. I can't show you because the building is standing in the way. There is a meadow here and then the entrance to the local community on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And, unfortunately, there is -- the other photograph is not available. But that place where you have drawn the red -- where you have marked it in a red line, can you just convert that into an arrow, pointing to where you think the air bomb landed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: It is behind this building down on the meadow behind this building or around this building, as you like. Some 50 metres from there, there is an entrance in this large building here. I just can't show you from this side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have gotten as much as you will get from her on issue, and I think the last statement is helpful. "Some 50 metres from there;" that is, from the point where she has marked red.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I, nevertheless, would like to tender this photograph into evidence, on account of the red marking there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P354, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, In answers to my learned friend in cross-examination, and for the benefit of the Defence I'm looking at page 39, line 6, Witness, the Defence counsel asked you -- her question was: "And towards Nedzarici there are also high-rises which are very similar to the ones that we see on the photograph, a great number of high-rises." And your answer was, and I quote: "If this is here was Alispasino Polje, this is where it was. I didn't go to Nedzarici. We did not dare to go to Nedzarici." And what I want to ask you is: Why did you not dare to go to Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Because of the shelling and because of the sniping, we just didn't go there; and then we didn't have any need to go there because we worked here. We helped other people taking water to them and firewood and making cooking ranges for them. I didn't go any -- anywhere, in fact. It was all demolished there. It was all destroyed there. There was sniping [Realtime transcript read in error "anti-sniping"]. There was shelling. No one dared go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, lastly, in your answers to my learned friend, you used the term "commander" when referring to the person that worked in the civil defence community or commune. Why do you use the term "commander"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: Well, the commander actually told us what to do. There was a roll call every morning to see whether we had all shown up, and we would be assigned so our tasks. Some people had to carry firewood; some had to carry tablets. We had to sign a list every morning at 8.00 to show that we were present, and he was our senior. We had to comply with his orders, and that is why we called him commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was the commander a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: No. No. He was an ordinary civilian, an elderly man in his 60s or so. Most of the people in fact were elderly people. I may have easily been the youngest among them. Most of the people were elderly. The UNPROFOR personnel know. They were right across the street from us. They know everything. They know about the air bombs and all these other things. They would come and give us fuel. They would help us take people to hospital if someone was wounded and so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your age, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the 16th of June, 1995, and in fact during the period August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, just before this gets off, in her answer to you earlier, she said, "There was sniping and there was shelling." The transcript has "anti-sniping and shelling," so I hope that will be corrected. Yes, please continue. That was in her answer as to why she didn't dare go to Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Does it need clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 107, lastly, the colleagues that you worked with in civil defence in Alipasino Polje and in particular on the 16th of June, 1995, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-107
utterances.text: They were all civilians; civilians, unfit people, elderly people. There was a person 70 -- there was a man 70 years of age. All of them were my peers, my generation. They were all civilians. We worked for the people, for the infirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness 107, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Waespi has the next witness. Might I be excused for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just two procedural matters. I should say that in Judge Harhoff's absence, Judge Mindua and myself sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Secondly, I take the opportunity to give a decision on the Prosecution's motion for admission into evidence of written statements of five witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Defence doesn't challenge the admissibility of the statements, but asks to be allocated reasonable time for cross-examination of the witnesses. On the 6th of March, the Trial Chamber granted the motion with regard to one witness, Rupert Smith, and admitted his statement into evidence. The Chamber now grants the motion with regard to the remaining four witnesses, and admits the statements of W-39, W-46, W-61, and W-150 into evidence, upon fulfilment of the requirements in 92 ter. As regards W-46, the originally estimated length of the examination was eight hours. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution indicated that it would reduce the overall length for the examination of W-46 to five hours through the filing of a 92 ter application. The Chamber, therefore, allocates two hours to the Prosecution and three hours to the Defence, and it will, at another time, set the times for cross-examination of the other witnesses. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one point, in relation to witness W-46, are you in a position to give at one time your decision about the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We issued that decision today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I need some time to switch my seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the meantime, the witness can make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. You may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Konings. Can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: My name is Harry Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: My current rank is lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is your function?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I am working in the Royal Netherlands Army as Chief of the Doctrine Division in the Land Forces Doctrine and Training Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And previously were you the head of office of artillery and mortar ammunition, and that relates to 1996?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In 1996, I held that position, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you also the commander of the fire support school?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I please make a remark about the two us speaking the same language, although it is a not our native language, but can you please stop for a moment before answering so the interpreters can catch up with us. And a good indication is, in fact, to follow the transcript in front of you. Once it has stopped moving then it is safe for you to answer. As the commander of the fire support school, what -- what was your job?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In that position, I was responsible for training all the fire support personnel of the Royal Netherlands Army. And with fire support, I mean everything in relation to artillery and mortars, fire support coordination, and fire support planning, so the whole fire support system of the Royal Netherlands Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was your training in -- in the army? Which branch did you initially belong to and were you trained in?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I was -- I was trained on the Royal Military Academy, that's a generic general training, which closes off in the last year with the specific weapons training; and in my case, that was at artillery school in the Netherlands. And from then on, I held various positions as an artillery officer in the Royal Netherlands Army. So my background is artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And does experience in dealing with artillery also include experience in dealing with mortar?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, since the fire support training school was also responsible for training of all mortar systems in the Royal Netherlands Army, including the Royal Netherlands Marines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the concept of crater analysis; and if so, can you tell us how you became familiar with that concept.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. The concept is allocated during our training on the artillery school, not very extensive. It's a course of, let's say, about one day; and during your operational tours and an operational units, you get familiar with that, since you pay visits to the training area, to the firing ranges in order to show your forward observers what the effects are of artillery and mortar projectiles. In fact, you go into the danger area when there is no firing and you show people what the effects are. Besides that, before I went to my UNMO mission, we had an extra training of, I think, it was half a day in our training on crater analysis; and upon arriving in Zagreb, we had an extra UNMO training and also there the UN paid attention to crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And very briefly, in theory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly then, Lieutenant-Colonel, the theoretical education in this matter was very short. Most of it was -- most of the learning that you have in this area was derived from practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before you went to Bosnia, and you explained us these fairly short training exercises, did you have theoretical education in dealing with crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. We had, as I told you, we had a short theoretical explanation during your artillery training, which was part of the military academy; and on various occasions during my operational time in various functions in the Royal Netherlands Army, we repeated that very briefly, and we put that in practice during firing exercises. After the firing exercises this closed, we went into the target area and showed our people how the craters look like and how the effects of mortar and artillery shells were. And we all based that -- no. I should say we all wrote it down in, what we called in the Netherlands army, so-called fire support bulletins, which are training documents available for all fire support personnel to keep up to date. And especially when more and more personnel got involved in the operation in 1992 onwards in Bosnia in UNPROFOR, we paid more and more attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you were in Bosnia for a while. Can you tell the Judges exactly for how long?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
