utterances.text: My period in Bosnia was from the -- I arrived in Zagreb at 30th of April, 1995. From there we were dispersed, my group of people was dispersed to various places. And on the 4th of May, I went to Sarajevo, and I stayed there until, I think it was the 26th or the 25th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was your function once you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The first few weeks, I was a team member of an UNMO team. After a few weeks, I became the position of department team leader; and after another few weeks, I became acting team leader and then team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us of which UNMO team were a team member? And I'm referring to your first assignment.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: When I came in, I was assigned to team Sierra Charlie 1, and " Sierra Charlie stands for "Sarajevo Central."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you became an acting team leader and then team leader, was that in relation to the same team?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was all in relation to the same team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us what team that was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The team was a very mixed team of most times consisting between six to ten UNMO of various nationalities. There were no two guys from the same nationality in one team. In my team, there were people from European countries, but there were also people from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Singapore, Indonesia, Egypt, all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where was the team located?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The team -- the team was located in the part of the Sarajevo which was called Sedrenik, which is, let's say, a habitat in the north-east part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you have an abbreviation for that team or the team location?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah. The team was called Sierra Charlie 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As a team leader, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As it was stated in the SOP, and SOP stands for standard operating procedure, of the UNMOs, in Bosnia, the team leader was in operational command of the UNMO team, which means that you were responsible for all the tasks UNMOs teams had to do. And the most important task was to be the impartial eye-witness of UNPROFOR inside the city of Sarajevo and give reports on every incident or every happening that occurred in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember when you became acting team leader of that Sedrenik team?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not quite sure about the dates, but it must have been somewhere at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you the team leader until you left towards the end of October?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's nearly correct. I handed over to a Norwegian colleague, I think about one week before I left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And whom did you replace as the team leader of that Sedrenik team of UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: My predecessor was a Danish captain. His name was Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I think it's -- I think his first name was Torban.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you think he was Danish? Do you know he was --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: He was Danish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How were you organized in your UNMO team that was stationed at Sedrenik during the time you were the acting and then the team leader?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We were acting in the following way: We had one team base which was in the Sedrenik area. It was -- the team base was based in -- in a room of a civilian house. And in the houses around the team base, the UNMOs had all their living facilities, which means that we were all living in between the civilian people, which is quite normal for UNMOs. They are in the middle of the civilian population. They are not on a military base so they can be approached directly by the civilians. Besides that, we had one observation post at the south part of the city quite high in the mountains, and that observation post was called OP1; just very plain, OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant-Colonel. We'll look at a map and a few photos shortly. Now, let me turn to your job as an UNMO and a team leader. Was part you are your duties to investigate into shelling and anti-sniping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how much of your work did that comprise, investigating shelling and sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It's very hard to -- to give, for example, a percentage to that, but there were periods when there was a lot of fighting going on that we -- that the only thing we did during the day was investigating and reporting shelling and sniper incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Your Honours how many investigations you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have been thinking that over, and I think it were at least 100 maybe up to 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did these investigations concern civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many of the investigations you conducted concerned civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I think that must have been at least between, let's say, 40 or 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were there specific locations where you investigated or specific areas where you realised that civilians would be targeted?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. There were certain areas that more often a point of shelling or sniping which were cross roads or water collection points, and especially cross roads when they were in view of the confrontation line. So it was easy to put a grid on that and make a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who would call you or task you to do these investigations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The task, the official task was always coming from UNMO HQ inside Sarajevo. We many times got first a call from the Sarajevo police, but we always had to get the permission to go on a certain location from our duty officers in the UNMO HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in which building was the UNMO HQ in Sarajevo stationed?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was the so-called PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And very briefly, how were these investigations conducted by you and your team UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: After a permission and after a call, we went to the location of the -- of the report. Most times we first picked up a one or more police officers of the Sarajevo police. We went to the spot, and we investigated what we saw, like a crater. We investigated craters. We looked for shrapnels, tails of mortars, and other evidence of the use of weapons. We took bearings, we noted grids; and after that we left the location as soon as possible, and we filed everything in a written report. And in the meantime, we gave a message on the radio to the UNMO HQ so that they were aware of what we had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you described the various activities of you and your UNMOs. How experienced were your fellow UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: There was a big variation between all the UNMOs. Some of them were already for a longer period in Bosnia. Some of them, just like I, had a background, an operational background which involved knowledge of artillery and mortars. But there were also new guys who had no experience with -- with the results and the effects of artillery and mortar fire or with the effects of snipering. So we had to teach all these guys, and we always send out patrols in combination of an experienced guy and a new guy together. So new guys never went alone on patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. You mentioned a few moments ago the Sarajevo police. Did the Bosnian police, the Sarajevo police also investigate into the same incidents you were investigating?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to Your Honours the cooperation you had between the Bosnian police and yourself?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Most of the time we had a good cooperation. We kept our investigations separate, which means they did their own thing and we did other own thing. There was just a matter of having the agreement that we went together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you exchange information?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We did exchange information, but I have to stress that it is -- was an exchange of information, not altering information. When we had a difference of information, we kept our own information as we discovered it, and we let them keep their own information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion about the professionalism of the Bosnian police you were working with or alongside?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In many of the occasions, I think they were quite professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us that were investigating -- I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before going on to another topic, I would like to ask one question. Witness, among the things you were doing on the field, you also talked about crater analysis, fragment research, or tried to also find the tail-fin of projectiles, et cetera. But I did not hear you talk to us about examination of wounds or corpses. Don't you think that type of examination would shed more light on the type of projectile used, and I'm asking this question because this courtroom very often, we hear talk about the fact that there were not enough bodies on the site, not even people killed. So is that part of your investigation as well? Were you investigating on the bodies found on the site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Part of our investigation was that afterwards we cleared the area where the shelling had occurred. We always went to the hospital and especially to the morgues to investigate the killed -- the killed people. This was an integrated part of your procedure, and we checked together with the Bosnian police we checked the number of killed people. We checked the kind of wounds that they had. And one other thing we were checking, we were obliged to check on order from our superiors whether the wounded were fresh, yes or no -- or the killed people were fresh, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for -- to check whether the wounded were fresh, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: There were rumours that people killed on one spot were dragged around the city and were planted on another spot apparently to -- to make the number of killed people looking higher than they were. And since there were rumours, and maybe they was strong rumours, I don't know that, we got the order from the senior military observer in Sarajevo that we had to check carefully whether this was happening, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you have personnel within your unit competent to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had -- we had no -- no specific trained personnel for that. And as the time went on, unfortunately, I can say that I became the more or less the only expert in my team to do that. So nearly all the investigations involving killed people, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did you make the determination that a person had been recently killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see that, I think, about the way -- the appearance of the wounds. You can see whether they are fresh or not the way the people are lying, whether they are stiff or not, et cetera. All that kind of things you can see. And, again, I'm not an expert in that, but have I seen dead people before I went to Bosnia. We had no special training for that; but in my first weeks in Sarajevo, I did all my work together with the then team leader, Captain Torban Hansen. And unfortunately we saw several killed people in that period; and from there, I got the experience I built up later on in my time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And following up on -- on Your Honours' questions and what you said, did you ever see what somebody would call planted evidence? Did you ever see an instance where you would form your opinion based on your experience gained on the ground that this evidence has been planted?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No. I never have seen that kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Now, what was the result of these investigations you and your team conducted, and I think you mentioned the number 100. Were you able to come to a conclusion as to the origin of fire of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In many of the cases, we were able to make the conclusion that they came from -- from Serb territory. Not all the cases we could make that conclusion, but, as I said, in many of the cases we could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how were you able to come to that conclusions as to the source of fire or direction of fire? What were the tools you could use to determine that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Before he answers that, may I just inquire from the lieutenant-colonel in those cases where you did not determine that the fire came from the Serbs, would I be right then in presuming that you determined that it came from the -- the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The firings we could not designate to a certain source, we left an undesigned [sic]. So we didn't know where they came from. That means that we had no evidence of fires coming out of Bosnian territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So had you no evidence of firing coming from Bosnian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I with recall in my period, I haven't seen it. There were firings from Bosnian territory, but not witnessed by my personally but by other UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you form an opinion at that time, and perhaps today, as to the tactics of the Bosnian Serbs in engaging their targets? And I'm talking about shelling.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I have an idea about that, and that's my personal opinion. And I do that with my background as a first time officer. I think in most of the times - I am not say in 100 per cent of the cases, but it comes very close - the use of the mortars, as it was done inside Sarajevo, was a matter of harassing fire, which means that you put it anywhere knowing that you will hit targets. And in most of the cases, there were no military targets involved because to my opinion there were very few real military targets inside the city of Sarajevo; and when you use a mortar inside an urban operation in the way it was used, it can infect lots of harm against, especially unprotected and unwarned civilian people. Military scene, a mortar is used in a different way than it was used in, let's say, 95 per cent of the cases inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Following up on your last sentence, how is it a mortar normally used in military sense?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Mortars, as well as artillery, belong to the military function, as we call it, fire support, and the word says it already. It is support with fire of combat troops in action, which means that they serve the purpose. When there is a combat action going on by infantry or by tanks or by reconnaissance troops, fire support units are supporting them by bringing in their strength and their flexibility to support the action, which is done. By doing that, you most times do that in certain procedures and very often or in most cases you use more than one or two or three rounds. You have a certain pattern in that. Mortars, especially, are area weapon systems, so they are not designed for pinpointing targets, that has to do with their design with narrow inaccuracy. So when you use mortar systems, you use them against an area target; for example, soldiers in an attack or soldiers in open terrain or that kind of targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. What kind of mortars did the Bosnian Serb army use in Sarajevo, according to your observations at that time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Most of the time, it was 120-millimetre mortars, and on some occasions they used 81 or 82. I'm not quite sure what calibre they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to Their Honours the impact of a 120-millimetre mortar. What effect does it have on the target?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the projectiles that were used were high explosive, which means the high explosive projectile is a steel or an iron case filled with an explosive, most times TNT; and on detonating, it produces shrapnels, thousands of shrapnels, and it produces a blast, a very high-pressured blast. It depends on where the projectile is landing, either in the open if it hits the building, so the effect is directly connected with the environment. The effect is also connected with the angle of impact of a projectile. And the effect is also connected, for example, with whether the detonation takes place in the open or in a closed area. So there are various factors that influence the ultimate effect of one projectile on -- on a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Were you at your team base, perhaps elsewhere, ever targeted by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, especially at the team base, we had various occasions that we were shot at from a ridge which was called Sharpstone. It was a quite common area where the Serb army had a perfect view into the territory of the Sedrenik area. And when we came back from patrol, on many occasions, they fired with machine-guns or sniper rifles over our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it possible that the Bosnian Serbs mistakenly fired at your team base or over your heads?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Everything is possible, of course, but or vehicles were clearly marked. They were white UN vehicles with a blue flag on it, with big black letters written on that "Military Observer," also in the Bosnian language "Vojni Promatraci." And our house was marked with various UN flags, so they were quite well to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the day you arrived at the team base?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why do you remember it very well?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, first, of course, it was a very specific day, being on a plane an UN plane, coming down in the minute from, let's say, 5.000 metres up to Sarajevo airport being thrown in an armoured car from the transport from the airport to the UNMO HQ, and from there up to the team base. And, secondly, a very specific experience was that after five minutes sitting outside the house, there was a sniper shot just about 30 centimetres over my shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how did you interpret that shot at that time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I personally did absolutely nothing because that was just to realise -- it took my time to realise what had happened, but my team leader, the Norwegian Captain Hansen who had been there for several months, I think at least five months, immediately came up with the conclusion that it was a sniper rifle shot from Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you one sentence about the situation in Sarajevo in general. You just explained the experience had you when you arrived in -- in Sarajevo at your team base. Can you tell Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says Norwegian, the Norwegian Hansen. Was there also a Norwegian Hansen or a Dane Hansen? Because the transcript says the Norwegian Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us hear what the witness said. Witness, how did you refer to Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Captain Hansen was the Danish Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Did the lieutenant-colonel say what his position was at that time when he was an UNMO, his position notice army? He replaced Captain Hansen. So at that time what was your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My position in the Netherlands Army was Lieutenant-Colonel, and I was head of the artillery and mortar ammunition office in the Directorate of Materiel, which means that in that period I was responsible for especially the techniques involved in procuring artillery and mortar ammunition and the use of that in the Netherlands Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I was about to ask you how the situation was in Sarajevo when you arrived. Was it full with soldiers? Was it busy with civilians? Can you give Your Honours an idea of the way Sarajevo looked?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In the period I arrived, there were many civilians inside Sarajevo, also fugitives from the area around Sarajevo. There were soldiers inside the city, but not in big groupings. There were small patrols on the street. And every night we saw, because we were quite close to the confrontation line, we saw the exchange of troops in the confrontation line. But there were no very big amounts of people. The life varied very much. There were days when it was quiet, and then you saw more people on the street because they had to do their daily business trying to get food, et cetera. And there were lots of very tense days with a lot of fire exchange between the Bosnian and the Serb army in the confrontation line and in the city. In general, my first four months there, the situation was quite tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Let's move to Markale. Were you involved in the investigation of what's now referred to as Markale 2, an incident that occurred on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when did you hear for the first time that something had happened at or near Markale?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: First time was when I was driving in my car. Coming back from the UNMO HQ on my way to my team base, I got the information on the UNMO radio net that there had been an explosion in the city and that there were probably numerous people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What did you do next? Did you continue to drive back to your team base, or did you stay in the city?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No. On that moment, since I was not too far away from the team base, I decided to drive back to the team base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you do at the team base?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Only after a few minutes, we got the phone call that -- from the police that they needed us for an investigation. And I decided immediately that I was the -- since I was the only available experienced UNMO that I should go there together with two colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who were these two colleagues?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Those were the Spanish Captain and a British Flight Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. The Spanish Captain was called Carbonell, and the British Flight Lieutenant was called Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you take material with you in order to conduct your investigation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. We always carried around our standard equipment needed by UNMO, which was fairly basic; of course, your helmet, flakjacket, compass, binoculars, medical kit, and your radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you go to the scene where the explosion occurred?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Not directly. We first stopped at the police station which had called us to go there, and we picked up some police officers; and from there, we went up to the scene of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your opinion, how long after the explosion had occurred did you and your colleagues arrive at the scene?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In my recollection, it must have been between, let's say, 30 and 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, approximately, at what time did the explosion occur?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was shortly after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please describe to Your Honours the scene that was in front of you. What did you see when you arrived at the scene of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: When we came there, there was a lot of glass on the street, literally centimetres of broken glass; lots of pools of blood; and lots of body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the situation like? What was the -- did you talk to people? Were they calm, agitated? Can you tell Your Honours how it was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The situation was extremely tense. A lot of people were on -- still on the street; of course, a lot of uniformed people, police officers, army people, but also civilians, and especially the civilians were shouting against us. They were very angry. And what my interpreter told me is that they were accusing the UNMOs or the UN, UNPROFOR for the fact that we that could have not avoided this, that we could have -- we didn't have the possibility to stop this kind of things to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned Bosnian police officers; in fact, you said uniformed people, police officers. Who were these police officers, these uniformed people?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do not know. We were accompanied by -- by uniformed and civilian people -- police officers were the same ones which with whom we were doing business all the time. And all the uniformed people, I do not know. I have not spoke with them as well, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because these were local, these were Bosnian uniformed personnel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also see international soldiers, members of UNPROFOR or other contingents?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. There were some other people on the scene. What I can recall is that they were French soldiers, French UNPROFOR soldiers on the scene, doing also an investigation. And I can recall that my superior, senior military observer, was very shortly on the scene of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was your senior military observer? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It was a Norwegian lieutenant-colonel, and his name was Oyen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We exchanged one sentence to each other. First thing he told me was put on my helmet was because I was wearing my beret, and he was right in that. And the second one was that he told me was that I not allowed to talk to anybody, to the press, or to anybody else, and that I had to remember the impartial status and the impartial way of working of the UNMOs, which meant that I was not allowed to say anything about the original of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you talk to any other people, apart from your boss, while you were at the scene of explosion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I talked, of course, to my direct colleagues; the Spanish captain and it's British lieutenant. And I talked to the people of the Bosnian investigation team which was formed just before that we started our work, which among other there is was a judge of the Sarajevo court, various police officers, some of them I already told you I knew already on that date. So I talked basically with my colleagues and Bosnian investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, what were you doing now on the ground? What was your task, and what did you do and your two colleagues do in investigating this incident?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Basically, we did not behave in another way than we did in any other incident, which means that we tried to collect as much data as we could: First of all, parts of the projectile; secondly, trying to, of course, find the crater; and then trying to find parts of the projectile; and then have a good look on all the things which are around, which are specific for that occasion. Because every occasion was different, so you look for every point you can find which is different. And at the end you write that down, and you have a first draft of your written report and then you have the most important data available. You talk on the radio to the UNMO HQ and tell them what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Among you and your two colleagues, Mr. Carbonell and Mr. Higgs, did you have a allocation of duties? Was somebody doing something specific while the other was doing something else?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, we shared tasks. I kept the overview and I kept a close eye on what the people of the Bosnian investigation team were doing; Let's say, tried to liaise with them, together with my interpreter. And Lieutenant Higgs used his compass and investigated the crater, and Captain Carbonell assisted him with that and measured also -- used also his compass and measured the distance between the crater and the wall of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you enter one of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We saw on the first floor all broken windows, some superficial damage inside the building, and we found some body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you were looking for parts of the projectile. Did you find parts of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. We found the tail of the projectile and we found also some shrapnel, but most important was the tail of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How far away from the crater was the projectile?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure anymore. I think it must have been between maybe ten, 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In what condition was the -- the part of the projectile? In fact, I should ask you: What part of the projectile was found?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We found the tail of the projectile, and you can recognise it very easy. We could read the inscriptions which are always in such a tail, which gives the detail on the manufacturer and the lot it is part of, and we could see that the tail-fins were bent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you form an opinion about the causes, the reasons while -- for the fact that the tail-fin was bent?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Not very specific, since in earlier occasions we found tail-fins which were also damaged; and when a projectile hits the ground, huge forces are coming around, and the material of which the tail-fins are made can be bent, I will not say easy, but can be bent. So it was not a specific thing what had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you say it was not a specific thing that this occurred, do you mean that it wasn't something unusual?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also talked about the crater. In what condition was -- was the crater, perhaps compared to other craters you have seen while you were in Sarajevo and indeed in Holland?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It was a very clear crater in the asphalt, in the concrete of the street and it was immediately to recognise being a crater coming from a mortar projectile, which is quite different from an artillery projectile. And it -- I had seen many of these craters before in the same condition in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I realise that I've almost eaten up an hour and that was the time originally allocated to me for examination-in-chief. I ask leave to, in fact, continue and I'm sure it will be another -- I hope to conclude it within the hour. Within the next hour, within 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, so you would have then taken almost two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's an underestimation of the time. This is becoming a feature of the case that the Prosecution underestimates the time. I am to say that the underestimation of the time will not affect the total, the global, time set for the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And I think occasionally we will make it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Going back to an earlier remark you made, Mr. Konings, when we talked about the tail-fin you have found, and you mentioned an inscriptions which featured the detail of the manufacturer. Do you remember who the manufacturer was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We found inscriptions in Cyrillic writing in the back of the tail, which gave an indication that they were either Warsaw parts produced or Serb produced. I'm not -- I do not know which factory exactly, but from that inscription number, the type of number, you can trace back the batch number of the projectile and the manufacturer, if you have the appropriate documentation with you, which we hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to turn your attention, the witness' attention, to Exhibit P265, this large board which is behind you, Lieutenant-Colonel. I think can we leave it there so everybody can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photo, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I recognise the photo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It depicts the location of the explosion on the 28th of August, as we have been talking about it before. It shows the crater which I have been analysing and investigating there and -- well, the area of -- the wider area of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you, perhaps with the help of your pointer there, point to the crater you just talked about.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The crater is -- I'm pointing that now. This is the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that you went to the inside, into the inside of a building. Do you see that building here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it has been this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Looking at the crater again, in your experience, did you see any indication, any signs, of tampering with the crater?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talked about the investigations you conducted with your colleagues. Did you come to a conclusion as to the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we came to a firm conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Their Honours your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Our conclusion was, as I can recall, it was 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please tell us again, how did you ascertain that it was 170 degrees? What was the basis for that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The basis for such a conclusion is that you try to follow the steps you take in crater analysis, which is very hard to do in concrete because the preferred methods are using sticks which you put into the ground. And the basic point is you try to divide the crater you see in equal patterns, in two equal patterns, and the middle line of these two equal patterns gives you the rough bearing of where the projectile came from. By using the stick method, as it's called, you can do it more precise, but since -- well, wooden poles, you are not able to fix wooden poles in concrete, and since you want to work fast in this tense situation, we did not use the stick method. But since it's a very clear crater, you can divide it in two halves, which we did, like this, and from there, you take with your compass bearing in the -- over the middle line of the two halves and that's your designated bearing you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we talked a little bit about crater analysis before the break. Is it a difficult undertaking? Is it a science? Or how do you feel about analysing these craters?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I would not describe it as a science, but you have to know the basics. You have to know the difference between artillery and mortar craters. From there you can work on the specifics of that. And you have to, of course, know how to handle the basics of sharing both halves and you have to be able to handle a compass in the right direction and to read that kind of stuff. So I wouldn't call it science. It's just -- it belongs to, more or less, basic military skills when you are an UNMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not rocket science.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not rocket science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the difference between mortar and artillery, can you just tell me what that difference is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The difference is that with an artillery projectile you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Not the -- it's an even more basic question. What is the distinction between artillery and mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in relation to the crater or in use or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, a mortar is a high-angle projectile, which means that you fire it with a high angle which mean that the projectile goes like this. Artillery is using a lower angle of fire, which gives artillery a much bigger range to reach and gives it also more accuracy than a mortar. There are much more differences between them, but I think these are quite some distinctive differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you, then, Colonel, also come a conclusion as to the angle of descent? In fact, I want to be more precise, to the minimum angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we calculated a possible minimum angle of impact, as we call it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And to what conclusion did you and your team come?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, from what I said, it was about 67 degrees impact angle, minimum impact angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Their Honours what this minimal impact angle means. In relation to what?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: When you have a minimum angle of impact, you can go into the firing table, which is a book in which every firing detail of a weapon system is stored, and for the different charges you can trace back the distance from where the projectile was fired. So that gives you a certain explanation from where, already, the origin of the weapon system was. But for that you need to know the charge which was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But let me go back to this angle. Can you tell us in relation to what was it, 67 degrees? What was coming in at an angle of 67 degrees?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It means -- this angle means the angle the projectile hits the street. So the projectile has hit the street under an angle of a minimum of 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And to have a reference number of 90 degrees would mean what?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It would be vertical down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours how you came to the conclusion that it was a minimum angle of 67 degrees?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very simple, mathematical method. You measure the distance from the crater, from the middle point of the crater, to the wall of the house, you estimate the height of the house, and you can, with a very simple mathematical method, you can calculate the minimum angle of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show Your Honours and the witness about 8-minute video which was shot at the time, around the time, the lieutenant-colonel was on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't think there is sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So please feel free, Lieutenant-Colonel, to make comments, especially when you see you or other personnel you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you hear the sound of glass? Is that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. You can see it on the video now, how much glass is on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you hope to get from this, Mr. Waespi, because it's pretty dreadful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honours, this is reality, and it will go on into showing the members of the various teams that come to investigate. You see the way the compass was used. I think it's important to show that to Your Honours and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have nothing against the showing of this, but what use can it be with this witness? Because when he came to the scene, he didn't see any of this. It cannot be of any use with this witness because the witness was on the spot when it happened. Otherwise I do not object to the showing as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we just move to the section of the video which is relevant to the witness. You said something about --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We can try to move quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In fact I'm stopping it. I think it is really awful and of very minimal evidential value.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we can do it from our desks, so not display it to the courtroom, if that can be done, we'll move quickly forward until to -- yes, we are here already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: These are French soldiers which were doing the UNPROFOR investigation, and on the back you can see a civilian walking with -- on the right side, that is myself, with the blue beret on the head, and the civilian next to me is my interpreter. And these, again, are the French UNPROFOR soldiers. That's -- on the left is Lieutenant Stephen Higgs, the British guy. The French are making preparations to do their investigation, and you see the three of us standing over there. Now we are measuring the distance I was talking about, between the impact and the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that measure would be used to determine what?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That would be used in combination with the estimation of the height of the building to estimate the minimal angle of impact. The left is the Spanish captain with, again, Lieutenant Higgs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were there any members of the government police force carrying out investigations with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same period that we were doing investigation, people of the Bosnian police, I'm not quite sure whether they were -- let's call it government representatives, were also doing their thing, let's put it that way. But I cannot recall what exactly they were doing because we were busy gathering our own details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were never investigating the same area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were investigating the same area and they were collecting, in all these cases, and also in this case, the same data as we collected, but we did it in a separate way. So I paid attention to my own work and not to the work that the Bosnians were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So when you came to a determination as to the direction from which the shell came, how was that arrived at in relation to the government police force? Was there any discussion with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that precisely. I'm sure we discussed that with them, but what is more important to me on that specific moment was that we compared our data, especially the bearing, with the French data, the French UNPROFOR data. That's what we did on the spot, to be sure that we had -- that we had a comparison with each other. And whether we compared that with the Bosnian investigation, I cannot recall that anymore. It was too busy at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what you see on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: What you see on the screen is the central area of the crater, which gives you the point where the projectile hits the ground, which is a kind of very small crater inside the big crater. Let's say that's the point of impact. And of course on the left-hand side you see a French soldier with his compass ready to take the bearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you and your colleagues and the French measure these data independently of each other and discuss it later, or did you have a joint measuring?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: What we did is that the compass bearing we did independent from each other. The measurement of the distance between the central part of the crater until the wall, the French measured because they had a special measuring device for that, and we checked it, whether we could agree with that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we -- maybe, for the record, this is at 5 minutes, 55 seconds, and it -- yes, just two minutes before the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's my hand checking with the French soldiers what is happening and what they were doing, because I speak a small -- a bit of French. And that's the scene as we found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe we can stop now the video, and please remove it from the screen. If that could be tendered into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this, Lieutenant-Colonel: Is what you found on the scene, the bodies, the shrapnel, the tail-fin, whatever you saw and experienced, is that consistent with what you told us earlier about the impact a 120-millimetre mortar can have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Remember that the -- remember that evidence has already been led about the impact of 120-millimetre mortar. I was anticipating your point, but, anyway, let me hear what have you to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I got the right interpretation, but Prosecutor Mr. Waespi suggested what you have found, bodies, and some other elements; whereas, I didn't hear from the witness that he himself had found a single body on the site. But if the interpretation was correct, Mr. Waespi seems to have said "bodies," suggesting something that the witness did not mention until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, did you find any bodies on the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you find shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found shrapnels, the tail, and body parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you found body parts but not bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not complete bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you found the tail-fin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Based on what you had found and seen on the crime scene, was that consistent with what you had described earlier as the impact of a 120-millimetre mortar could be?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is consistent with what I think a 120 projectile can do, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know how many victims there were, how many dead people?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: During that day, the number varied; but as I can recall, at the end of the day, there were, I mean, 38 victims, dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We're jumping ahead a little bit. Did you go to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, on that moment, I think we got about 35 -- we counted about 35 killed people. They were all lying in the morgue which, at the time was a big concrete cellar with nothing in it, no tables, or no furniture at all. People were lying on the floor; and as I have told before, you could see very clearly that they were very recently killed, because blood was still coming out of their wounds and the way they were lying, you could see that they were recently killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did you go to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That must have been shortly between 12.00 and 1.00. I cannot be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's on the same day, on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And let me go back to my earlier point. Is the result of 38 victims, dead people, consistent with what you had described earlier as a possible impact of a 120-millimetre mortar fired at that specific location?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I think it's consistent. Yeah, I'm convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could have the -- Exhibit P85, which is 65 ter 00198, a patrol report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I see a copy of the handwritten patrol report of the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is a patrol report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: After -- after every patrol, according to the UNMO regulations, we had to write a written statement which is the patrol report, in which you have the opportunity to write down every single detail you saw, you discovered during your patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you can tell us who wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This report was written by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what it contains specifically.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It contains a summarized description of the facts we saw during that day, especially during the investigation in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And does it contain under "Observations," in the middle of the page, under the first subheading 1, a remark about the bearings, the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now paragraph 2, if you could read that to -- to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. "The bearings in combination with the estimated angle of impact could give no evidence on the origin of fire since not is it none with which charge the projectile -- the projectile has been fired."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to Their Honours what that means?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That means exactly as it says, that on the -- on the moment that we were on the spot and on the moment that I wrote this report, that we could not establish evidence of the origin of fire. We could establish a bearing, a direction from where the firing came from, but we could not give any evidence on the origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is needed to come to a conclusion as to the origin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: If you have the estimated angle of impact and if you have a bearing, then you -- the only other thing you need to know is the charge with which the projectile was fired. Because to every charge there is an a set of distances connected; and when you have the angle of impact of 60, 70 degrees and you know which charge it is, you can directly connect it to an estimated distance, and then -- and then you can -- you can come up with a possible origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was it not possible to ascertain the charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You cannot find out the charge that was fired because you have no evidence on the -- the spot of the explosion where the shell lands of any charge anymore of the. You cannot see that. Unless you have a highly sophisticated technical available, which can only be done in the factory, maybe with whatever equipment you have available to find out how many traces of -- the powder, gun powder is on the tail. But we did not have any possibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you receive other information which allowed you to make a determination as to the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. We had on the same moment that -- no, I should said -- rephrase that. Our OP1 in the south part of the city, in the mountains, was manned 24 hours a day by two UNMOs. They covered the complete area of the city. They could see the complete -- nearly the complete city of Sarajevo, especially to the north and the west part. And the day of the 28th of August, the weather was very clear, very sunny, very bright. There was hardly any wind, and there was -- it was very quiet so there were no battle noises, no firing during that morning, which means that any firing from there area where our OP1 was located, especially from a 120 mortar, would have been seen or heard by the UNMOs on the OP1. And that, in combination with the bearing, gave us the conclusion that the origin of fire must have been behind the mountains, so inside Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talked about OP1, which was in the south part of the city in the mountains. Were you ever at OP1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have been on OP1 on many occasions and fulfilled also these 24-hour duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who gave you the information that there was no firing during that morning?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That information came direct to me from the two UNMOs on OP1; Lieutenant Commander Thom Knustad and Major Paul Conway?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: They told us that there was no outgoing round from their facility, no outgoing round from any type, so not 120, from their broader vicinity; not only the direct vicinity, but I'm talking now about the broader vicinity which is -- well, if you look on the map, it goes up to nearly one kilometre or maybe even behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a chance to look at a photo in a moment. How professional were the observes that you on OP1 that day, and you mentioned Mr. Knustad?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Especially he was already a longer period in Sarajevo. He was at that period already designated to be my successor as a team leader, and he succeeded me when I left. And he also, just like I am was an artillery man, a Norwegian coastal artillery, so he had more or less the same experience with the use of artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And tell us again the significance of Mr. Knustad and his colleague not hearing any outgoing round at that time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, it -- it is the missing clue in -- in trying to designate the origin of fire of that specific round. In case it would -- the round would have been fired from Bosnian army territory, it the round would been done -- in combination with this minimum angle of impact, it would been done with charge zero, the lowest charge you can fire. If you trace that back from the origin of impact, you would have come in the area around OP1. The place of origin of fire would have been in the area around OP1. And since on that quiet day you cannot miss, to my professional opinion, an outgoing 120-millimetre round, it's a loud bang. You cannot miss it, you will see it, you will see the flash, you will see the smoke. Well, that brings you to the conclusion that the round came from further away; and since there was no noise heard, it must have been come from behind the mountain ridge, which is on the south side of the city of Sarajevo, which muffles the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can pull up, Mr. President, exhibit 65 ter number 00197, and it should be a map displayed shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember having signed a map which was attached to your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I did remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a coloured map. That's why it takes a little longer, Mr. President, Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that the map you can displayed here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It is that map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see a marking OP1?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And with the help of the usher you could circle around that marking, and attach, please, the letter A next to it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you also see a marking depicting the team base?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please circle it and attach letter B next to it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that could be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, that day, 28th August 1995, did you before the shell exploded already pass by Markale on that morning?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why did you pass by Markale?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It's located in the main street of the central city -- of the central part of the says of Sarajevo, and it was part of our patrols and I had a habit, as a team leader, that I went every morning for a visit to the UNMO HQ at the PTT building, just to have a short talk with my -- with the senior military observer and to check with the OPs officers, whether there were specific details that we needed to know. So I passed there during that morning between, I think, 9.00 and 10.00 on the later on where the explosion took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that was roughly one or two hours before the explosion. Can you tell Their Honours what you saw while passing by that location?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite crowded in comparison with other days. A lot of people on the street, most civilians, the usual activity of patrolling police officers and some military; and especially in that reasonable narrow part of the street, there were lots of people on the sidewalk. People were selling goods or trading, changing goods to have money to buy food, et cetera, et cetera. So it was quite crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you talk about the sidewalks, are you talking about the exact location which you see displayed behind you on that board?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. That was part of the sidewalk, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, driving past did you have any thoughts about these people being gathered there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, I had some strange thoughts about that, because as we had it before that when people gathered and firing occurred that people get killed. So I didn't trust the situation that morning. It's just an emotional feeling, but I had the idea this is not right. It is too quiet and there are too many people on the streets. There is no evidence for that, and it's just feeling and my experience you after five months in such a city, but that was my feelings on that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me conclude this part asking you since you were there before and after the explosion, was it possible to stage this scene, to drag dead bodies to the scene?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In relation to what I saw in the morning when I passed there, I'm convinced that is not possible to stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, in the morning, there was no crater on the street. I'm absolutely sure of that, so that means you have to create a crater. Have you to create, to make artificially a crater, like what you see on the photograph. I don't think you can make that in short time frame between my first appearance there and then later on. Secondly, to create that other chaos which was there, in the middle of a crowd of people who are trying to -- to live on, trying to get some food, to my opinion, that is impossible, to create such a situation without people asking questions or protesting against that. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier that some 30 minutes elapsed between the time you received the report and the time of your arrival. Wouldn't that have been enough time for bodies to have been moved to that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will not say that it is impossible to do that in 30 minutes; but, again, seeing the amount of people that were inflicted by -- on that moment on that morning, seeing in the morgue the freshness of the body, you must have -- you should have get them somewhere. There were no reports that morning whatsoever that there were at least 35 people killed on another spot in the vicinity of Sarajevo at all. And, again, there was no crater before I came -- when I drove there that morning. I'm convinced that in combination with what you saw, the bodies that I saw, the chaos that was created, civilians that -- the number of civilians that was walking around before on the street, that this is impossible to stage it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, if you just take a look at the Prosecution exhibit to your rear, to the back, that's the -- amidst that picture of destruction, we see two bicycles in what appears to be in a wholesome condition, not damaged. Do you remember seeing those bicycles when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't remember that anymore, no. I have no idea whether they were there, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was a reference to Prosecution Exhibit P265.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you investigate the impact of four other shells that impacted in the vicinity of Markale?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us as brief as you can, about that investigation. That investigation was done in the afternoon; I think it was around 2.00. There were four other impacts. Two of three of them were in an open concrete parking lot, and one of them -- at least one of them was in the top of a building of a -- I think it was a -- a business apartment building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you personally conduct the investigation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, with the same team as we did the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were there any casualties involved?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I can recall there were a few casualties, but I'm not quite sure how many anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you investigate into the direction of fire these four shells came from?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the result of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was -- I mean, that we said between 220 and 240 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember whether you came to a conclusion as to what calibre, indeed what mortar, these shells were fired from?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We came to the conclusion that it was also 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was the impact in relation to the Markale impact? How far away?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It was on the other side of the block behind Markale in southern direction, roughly southern direction, and I estimate there were a few -- maybe 200 metres between the Markale impact and the other impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you come to a conclusion as to -- from which territory these four shells were fired?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, we didn't make a firm conclusion on that. So we just could make the bearing and that we couldn't make any origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now turning to the next day, 29th of August, 1995, were you involved in activities in relation to the Markale 2 investigation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. On the 28th, the leader of the Bosnian investigation team, a judge of the supreme court in Sarajevo, asked me whether I could be an observer in the investigation team, and I got information from my superior officer to do that. So on the 29th of August, I was in the meeting, in several meetings that took place in Sarajevo on -- on the further investigation of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you also involved in a briefing at the UNMO headquarters in that morning?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who briefed whom?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: On the 29th in the morning, we had our regular team meeting at the UNMO HQ under the direction of our senior military observer, and he asked me to give a briefing of what happened on the 28th of August to my colleague team leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Your Honours what you told your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Basically I went through the patrol report, and we discussed a lot of professional details, so I cannot recall every detail anymore, but it was a discussion between professional soldiers about what happened or what could have happened and the way we looked against it, and it was also a -- a learning discussion, since nobody of us had ever in that period had such an experience, so it was also a learning thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was peculiar about the experience you had?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, the peculiar thing is not the happening itself but the -- well, the sheer impact it had. Let's say in military terms, we call it the effect it had. And the effect was much -- much bigger than any of us in that period had -- had ever seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you talk to other people outside the group of team leaders and your chain of command about your findings in relation to Markale 2?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Just inside my own team. The extra people I talked about the Markale incident were the -- were my own UNMOs in my team in Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you talk about the effect being bigger than anything that you had seen previously, what do you mean? Are you just referring to the number of persons who were killed and injured? Or what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I am talking about the effect, I was thinking about that day or the day after when I was talking to the team leaders. We were discussing the sheer amount as you are referring to. So that means 38 killed people and nearly 100 wounded. When I talk about the effect, being the person I am today, I talk also about the indirect effects that that projectile had on the -- on the further development politically and military scene after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you told us you were to attend a meeting with the Bosnian police on the 29th of August. What kind of meeting was that, and what was your involvement?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I said, it was -- there was a special investigation team formed by the -- by the Bosnian authorities. They already started to have a meeting on the 28th in the afternoon and in the evening. I was also present then. And the idea was that they were collecting all relevant information in relation to that impact, pictures, shrapnels, any other evidence you -- you can think about. So they were putting together a complete report for the Bosnian authorities, and what the intention was to do with that report, I cannot -- I have no idea about that. But -- and I was a part of the meeting. As I told you, I was an observer, so I didn't take part in the discussions, although people tried to -- to -- to get me so far that I came up with certain statements they would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break now. We'll resume tomorrow at 2.15. -- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
